catalog_locator: Hedinger 1984 p. 223 (ch. 5, PM-PB vowel correspondences, paragraph after examples (59)-(65)); file. Éwané 2016 tone chapter paras 13 and 18
catalog_quote: From the PB roots and PM tones, it is clear that a second vowel must have been present in noun stems. Many of these vowels have been lost before and others since PM (cf. also 3.3.4 and end of 6.4.2). This may be described as a general trend which has been taking place over a long period of time. There appears to be no specific cause for this loss but it could possibly have to do with stress on the stem initial syllable. However, since tone is the main suprasegmental phenomenon which has distinctive function, stress is not often discussed and therefore the relationship of tone and stress is not well understood.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The Manenguba languages (Mbo included) are tone languages; tone is the only suprasegmental with distinctive function. Stress has not been described: Hedinger only speculates that a stress on the stem-initial syllable might explain the historical loss of second stem vowels (V2) in noun stems, and states explicitly that the relationship of tone and stress is not well understood. No source opened locates word stress in Mbo.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the remark is hedged ('could possibly') and made for Proto-Manenguba / the cluster as a whole, not for Mbo specifically.
new_statements.domain_note: Cluster-level comparative-historical remark about noun stems (stem-initial syllable), not a synchronic description of Mbo word stress. The modern reference grammar, Éwané 2016 (Mbo of Mbouroukou, Melong), is entirely silent on stress/accent: its tone chapter (pp. 71-80) posits five tones (H, L, HL, LH, and a 'ton moyen' of syntactic origin) and states 'Toute syllabe de la langue mbo porte l'une de ces marques tonales' (para 13), with lexical and grammatical functions; no word about intensity or prominence in the vowel, consonant, tone or syllable-structure chapters. Hedinger et al. 1981 (Mwaneka/Baneka variety) likewise gives only four tone marks and no stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog mboc1235 'Mbo (Cameroon)' covers Hedinger 1984's north-eastern group: Mbo of Ekanang/Mbouroukou [MBE], Mbo of Mboebo/Kekem [MBM], Mbo of Ngwatta [MBN]. Éwané 2016 describes 'le mbo de Mbouroukou', arrondissement de Melong (= MBE) and claims its results hold for the ~20 Melong village dialects. The Hedinger 1984 stress remark is made for Proto-Manenguba / the whole cluster, not for Mbo alone. Hedinger, Ekandjoum & Hedinger 1981 'Petite grammaire de la langue mboó', which Glottolog files under mboc1235, in fact takes 'le parler de Nkongsamba (le baneka)' as reference dialect (p. 5) and Hedinger 1984: 48 calls it 'a brief summary of aspects of Mwaneka grammar' — Mwaneka/Baneka [MWK] belongs to the Central-Eastern cluster (Bantu A.15g, with Bakaka, Balondo, Manehas), i.e. probably Glottolog's Central Mbo/Kaka (ISO bqz) rather than mboc1235; glottocode of that dialect not verified here.

sources.note: Silent on stress/accent/intensity in all five phonology chapters (présentation, vocalique, consonantique, tonal, structure syllabique). Tone chapter: five tones (haut, bas, descendant, montant, moyen), 'Toute syllabe de la langue mbo porte l'une de ces marques tonales' (para 13); lexical, grammatical, 'contrastive' and 'démarcative' functions of tone. Describes Mbo of Mbouroukou, arrondissement de Melong (ch. Présentation, para 33). OpenEdition Freemium: HTML full text open.

sources.note: Pedagogical sketch; phonology limited to the alphabet page (p. 6): four tones (ton haut, ton bas non-marqué, ton montant, ton descendant); no stress statement ('accent' occurs only as 'accent aigu' = high-tone mark, p. 51). Reference dialect 'le parler de Nkongsamba (le baneka)' (p. 5) = Hedinger 1984's Mwaneka [MWK], Central-Eastern cluster, not the north-eastern Mbo. downloaded via the Internet Archive (sil.org could not be reached by automated download).
